doc.title: Jane Monheit interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 20, 2010

title: Critics focus on her looks
summary: Reviews comment on her appearance and hair rather than the music, unlike treatment of men; being called 'ordinary'.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: What about the C word, the critics?

Generally they have more to say about my looks than they do about my music, which drives me nuts. And it goes in both directions. You know I’ll have reviews that — I was talking about this in an interview just yesterday. I’ll have reviews that focus on how hideous I looked than I sounded; and reviews that focused more on how great I looked than how I sounded. And I disagree with them. I tend to agree with the hideous-sayers. But yeah, it’s ridiculous. I mean what, just because I’m a young woman like that you’ve got to decide to pick that apart? I mean I know it’s what we do in this industry. It’s what we do. It’s part of it. But I feel like what we’re doing up there musically is good enough that that should take precedence over what dress I’m wearing and how much the critic liked the way it fit me, or what I did with my hair that night. People go crazy over the fact that my hands are always in my hair. Even just doing this interview right now I have my hands in my hair every second. It’s just a habit. It drives them nuts. I have people emailing my management asking me not to do it. I’m just like really, this matters this much?
You know they don’t do that with men singers. They don’t comment. I mean they might say well Joe Williams that night looked marvelous in his tux. But then that’s pretty much it.

Yeah. And instrumentalists never. And I enjoy the dressing up and the glamour and all of that. It’s super fun, I mean I love it, it’s really fun. But at a certain point though it’s like come on, really? This is what you’re going to talk about?

Well you know they have to have, I’ve often thought about critics and so forth, they have to have something to write about. And if they’re not really good at — if they’re not musicians first, which most of them are not, then it’s a little harder to write — it’s probably easier to write about how you look than the music part of it.

Yeah. And I mean the visual is important. Everyone is sitting there looking at you and they all have their opinions about it. Although it really does break your heart when somebody insults the way you look. I mean it really hurts. Of course it does. That never goes away. But the worst is when, like one times recently — well no, I hate it more when people insult my looks. That really hurts my feelings a lot. But recently I had someone say that my singing was “ordinary.” And that was just so mean that I laughed out loud when I read it. Because what other reaction was I going to have to something that was like that mean, to be called “ordinary.” Not like well she’s doing something but I don’t like it. That’s fine. But to be called ordinary. That was — I disagree.
That is rather a low blow.
Yeah but I seriously just started laughing because I couldn’t — I mean people have said a lot of bad things about me but they’ve never just said like eh.
